contributions.headingText: Lipomatosis of nerve is a benign tumour characterized by overgrowth of mature fibroadipose tissue within the epineurium, surrounding and separating nerve fascicles.
Acceptable: fibrolipomatous hamartoma; lipofibromatous hamartoma; macrodystrophia lipomatosa.

Lipomatosis of nerve typically involves appendicular nerves and occurs more frequently in the upper extremities (74%) than in the lower extremities (17%). The peripheral nerves most frequently affected include the median nerve (63%), plantar nerve (11%), and ulnar nerve (7%) {23684521; 30925468; 30798481}. Occasionally lipomatosis of nerve can be bilateral, affect multiple terminal nerves, or be restricted to the plexuses. Rarely, cranial nerves {38090637} and nerves along the axial spine {24506247} may be involved, but intradural involvement does not occur {35224812}.

Sensory loss and paraesthesias are the most common symptoms (accounting for nearly half of patients’ reported symptoms), followed by pain and muscle weakness {30925468}. Median nerve entrapment at the carpal tunnel most commonly accounts for neurological symptoms in median nerve lipomatosis of nerve. Overgrowth in the nerve distribution territory has been reported in > 60% of definite cases, especially in the upper extremities, with digital enlargement due to increase of soft tissue and skin and frequently true macrodactyly with enlargement of bone {30925468}. Although rare cases with isolated macrodactyly have been reported, occult lesions of lipomatosis can be identified upon examination of the proximal segments of the affected nerves {36624631}. On MRI, characteristic imaging features include a coaxial cable–like appearance on the cross-sectional and spaghetti-like appearance on the longitudinal plane.

A systematic review identified 618 definite cases of lipomatosis of nerve. Patients typically present in the first decade of life (> 60%), with only 10% of cases coming to clinical attention after the fourth decade of life. Sex distribution was balanced between male (49%) and female patients (51%) {30925468}.

Thought to represent a hamartomatous fibroadipose tissue overgrowth, lipomatosis of nerve is often progressive and behaves in a benign tumour–like fashion. It is sporadic. There are no syndromic associations except rare cases reported in association with Klippel–Trénaunay syndrome {3351231; 19411473} and Proteus syndrome {36177257}. Associated nerve-territory overgrowth seems to occur most frequently when lipomatosis of nerve occurs in motor and sensory nerve territory, suggesting that distal overgrowth may be influenced by the type of axons carried by the nerve {30798481}.

PIK3CA activating hotspot mutations have been reported in lipomatosis of nerve, with or without associated nerve territory overgrowth including macrodactyly {23100325; 29661094; 31481664; 35224812; 37067587}. These mutations are somatic and probably occur in mesodermal cells {35224812}. Lipomatosis of nerve is considered within the PIK3CA-related overgrowth spectrum of disorders, which also includes CLOVES syndrome (congenital lipomatous overgrowth, vascular malformations, epidermal naevi, and scoliosis or skeletal/spinal anomalies), muscle hemihypertrophy, megalencephaly–capillary malformation syndrome (MCAP), and others {31481664; 33089450; 25557259; 32692051; 36729078; 35256403; 37949664; 27426476}.
Lipomatosis of nerve causes a yellow, lobulated, fusiform enlargement of a peripheral nerve and at times its branches.

On transverse section, the epineurium is markedly expanded by mature adipose tissue and to a lesser extent by fibrous tissue; the nerve fascicles are widely spaced. Fascicles frequently show perineurial thickening and at times endoneurial septation with pseudo–onion bulb–like hypertrophic change, mimicking intraneural perineurioma and probably representing reactive changes to nerve compression. Moderate to severe nerve fibre loss may be present. Immunohistochemical studies for EMA, S100, and NFP may help in characterizing nerve fibre pathology.

Where cytological confirmation of a diagnosis is required, aspirated material would show tissue fragments of adipocytes containing a single large, clear cytoplasmic vacuole with a compressed rim of cytoplasm and a small nucleus with an inconspicuous nucleolus.
PIK3CA activating hotspot mutations are detected in a subset of cases.

Essential: coaxial cable–like appearance on cross-sectional imaging; epineurial expansion by mature adipose tissue with widely spaced nerve fascicles; perineurial thickening and pseudo–onion bulb–like hypertrophic change.

A benign condition, lipomatosis of nerve may require symptomatic treatment, including nerve decompression (e.g. carpal tunnel release for lipomatosis of distal median nerve) or variable degrees of excision, balancing preservation of nerve function and soft tissue debulking and/or bony procedures to address functional and cosmetic issues.
